draft.title: Elaborating ideas
card: To elaborate is to expand an idea so the reader understands it fully. A bare statement such as "The market was busy" leaves the reader to guess what you mean.
Example
shows the idea in a real case. "The market was busy: three people queued at every stall."
Explanation
says why or how. "The market was busy because school holidays began the next day."
Detail or comparison
A detail adds something the reader can picture, such as sounds or colours. A comparison links the idea to something familiar: "The market buzzed like a beehive."
draft.remember: Elaborating means adding an example, explanation, detail or comparison to an idea.

a.q: Which sentence elaborates the idea "Our school library is a quiet place" by adding an explanation?
opts: It is quiet because students must whisper and work alone
It is quiet, like a room where everyone is asleep
It is quiet, and I like going there to read
It is quiet, so it is a place that has little noise
a.why: The first option says why the library is quiet, so it is an explanation. The second is a comparison, not an explanation. The last option only repeats the idea in other words and adds nothing new.
a.clue: Look for the option that gives a reason.

b.q: Priya writes: "Our cat is clumsy." She adds: "Last week she pulled the curtain down on herself." What does the added sentence do?
opts: It gives an example of the clumsiness
It gives a comparison for the clumsiness
It gives a reason for the clumsiness
It repeats the idea in different words
b.why: The added sentence describes one real case of the cat being clumsy, so it is an example. It does not compare the cat to anything else, and it does not say why she is clumsy. It also adds new information, so it is more than a repeat.
b.clue: Does the sentence show one real moment?
